content: Development agencies should establish and execute policies that promote the safe use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater in agriculture and aquaculture. These policies should be integrated into their broader goals of conserving natural resources and reducing poverty. The rules governing international trade in food were established during the Uruguay Round of Multilateral Trade Negotiations and apply to all members of the World Trade Organization (WTO). Regarding food safety, these rules are outlined in the Agreement on the Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures. According to this agreement, WTO members are entitled to implement legitimate measures to protect the health and safety of their populations from food-related hazards, provided these measures are not unjustifiably restrictive to trade. Documented cases have shown that the importation of contaminated vegetables has led to disease outbreaks in recipient countries. Guidelines for the international trade of food products irrigated with wastewater should be based on scientifically sound principles of risk assessment and management. The WHO Guidelines for the Safe Use of Wastewater, Excreta, and Greywater in Agriculture and Aquaculture are grounded in a risk analysis approach, which is internationally recognized as the fundamental methodology for developing food safety standards. These standards aim to ensure adequate health protection while facilitating international food trade. Adherence to these guidelines in the production of food products intended for export will help ensure the unimpeded international trade of safe food products. This requires a robust monitoring process to ensure compliance with risk management measures and appropriate quality control from wastewater generation to the consumption of produce. These monitoring procedures should be embedded in national policies and regulations for water quality, including drinking water, recreational water safety, and general water safety plans. The health risks most commonly studied in the context of using wastewater, excreta, and greywater are those associated with excreta-related infectious diseases. There is less extensive evidence regarding the transmission of vector-borne diseases and schistosomiasis through reuse activities in agriculture, aquaculture, and general excreta and greywater use. The planning and development of projects involving the use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater in agriculture and aquaculture should include a health impact assessment or an environmental impact assessment with a strong health component. National environmental and health impact assessment policies should explicitly address these types of projects and their associated risks in their screening criteria. The scoping of such projects should include identifying vulnerable groups. Three community groups are at risk from wastewater, excreta, and greywater use in agriculture and aquaculture: farm or pond workers (and their families, if they participate in the activities or live on-site), local communities in close proximity to these activities, and consumers of the products. In regions with poor sanitation and hygiene conditions where untreated wastewater and excreta are widely used in agriculture, intestinal worms pose the most frequent health risks. Other excreta-related pathogens, such as those causing diarrhea, typhoid, and cholera, as well as parasitic protozoa and viruses, may also pose significant health risks. In countries with higher sanitation and hygiene standards and well-managed wastewater treatment infrastructure, viral illnesses pose greater health risks than other pathogens. This is partly due to the difficulty of removing viruses during wastewater treatment and their environmental resistance and infectivity at low concentrations. Additionally, populations in these regions often lack prior exposure to viral pathogens, resulting in no acquired immunity and increased vulnerability to viral infections. Studies on health risks associated with waste-fed aquaculture are limited. There is some evidence linking exposure to waste-fed aquaculture or its produce to illnesses in consumers and local communities in close contact with contaminated pond waters. Skin diseases, such as contact dermatitis, may occur in farmers who frequently handle fecally contaminated ponds while harvesting aquatic plants. Fish and plants raised in contaminated waters may passively transmit pathogens on their surfaces to handlers or consumers. Of greater public health importance is the fact that fish concentrate bacteria and other microbes, including viruses and protozoa, in their intestines. The greatest risk to consumers arises from cross-contamination of edible fish flesh with gut contents during unhygienic fish processing, which can increase microbial contamination levels by 100-fold or more. In certain regions, foodborne trematodes pose significant health risks related to waste-fed aquaculture. In areas where infections such as clonorchiasis, opisthorchiasis, fascioliasis, and fasciolopsiasis are common and where fish or plants are frequently consumed raw, incidence rates can be attributed to this practice. In vulnerable groups, such as children, foodborne trematodes can cause severe illness and, occasionally, death. Various animals may serve as reservoirs, sustaining the presence and transmission of these infections in affected areas. A recent systematic review indicates that foodborne trematode infections are on the rise in areas where freshwater aquaculture is also increasing. The risks associated with the use of excreta, including source-separated urine and feces, primarily stem from excreta-related pathogens. Urine generally contains low concentrations of pathogens but may have some due to fecal cross-contamination during collection. An exception to this is the eggs of the parasitic blood fluke Schistosoma haematobium. The use of fecal matter from on-site sanitation installations, such as septic tanks and pits of unsewered family and public toilets, poses significant health risks if not adequately treated. The primary health hazard arises from the presence of worm eggs in areas where intestinal worms are common. These eggs can survive for months or even years in fecal matter and soil. The health risks associated with using greywater in agriculture are considered lower than those for wastewater or feces. Greywater generally contains lower concentrations of pathogens but may still harbor some, introduced through activities such as washing babies’ diapers, laundry, personal hygiene, or other sources. Risk management is facilitated by analyzing the entire production cycle, from waste generation to product consumption. This knowledge is used to identify health protection measures that can reduce risks at different points to achieve agreed health-based targets. Public health policies should ensure the application of the most cost-effective measures in specific contexts. Measures may include wastewater treatment, crop restrictions, improved irrigation methods, protective equipment, produce washing and cooking, vector control, and immunization. Determining the cost-effectiveness of these measures under local conditions requires economic analysis, for which engaging a health economist is recommended. Developing and maintaining a national policy framework for the safe use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater involves a step-by-step, iterative process. This process should address the formulation and mainstreaming of new policies and the adjustment and harmonization of existing ones. A productive policy dialogue among all stakeholders is central to this process. Steps include establishing a mechanism for ongoing policy dialogue, defining objectives, conducting situation analysis and needs assessment, securing political endorsement, and engaging in research.
